title: Architectural design and the brain: Effects of ceiling height and perceived enclosure on beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions
research_question: To examine the effects of ceiling height and perceived enclosure on aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions in architectural design, and to explore their neural correlates using fMRI.

participants.description: 12 females, 6 males; M = 23.39 years, SD = 4.49; neurologically healthy; normal or corrected-to-normal vision; right-handed.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies volunteers for an fMRI study.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 200 photographs of architectural interior spaces, divided into four conditions: open high ceiling, open low ceiling, enclosed high ceiling, and enclosed low ceiling (50 images per condition). Stimuli were also balanced for curvilinear/rectilinear contour.

findings.mechanism: Higher ceilings might facilitate greater levels of visuospatial exploration and attention.
findings.quote: Specifically, participants were more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they had high than low ceilings.

findings.mechanism: Beauty judgment and approach-avoidance decisions might be underwritten by different sets of considerations and computations.
findings.quote: In contrast, rooms with higher ceilings were no more likely to be entered than rooms with lower ceilings

findings.mechanism: Open rooms afford a greater degree of perceived visual and locomotive permeability, which is linked to aesthetic pleasure.
findings.quote: Specifically, participants were more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they were open than enclosed

findings.mechanism: Enclosed spaces might elicit an emotional reaction (e.g., fear) that accompanies exit decisions, consistent with survival-related hypotheses.
findings.quote: and more likely to opt to exit them if they were enclosed than open.

mechanisms: Visuospatial exploration and attention (dorsal stream, MTL) for ceiling height effects on beauty judgments.
Processing of abstract representations derived from visual motion information (lateral temporal lobes) for perceived enclosure effects on beauty judgments.
Emotional reaction (fear) mediated by the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) for perceived enclosure effects on approach-avoidance decisions.
Neural dissociation between 'liking' (beauty judgment) and 'wanting' (approach-avoidance decisions).
implementation_implications: Architectural designers should consider ceiling height and perceived enclosure as important variables influencing aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
Higher ceilings are preferred for beauty, while open spaces are preferred for beauty and approach. Enclosed spaces are associated with avoidance.
Design choices can elicit specific neural responses related to spatial processing and emotional reactions, which can inform design for user experience.
limitations: Stimuli were not controlled for variables such as light, color, etc., to increase ecological validity, which might introduce confounding factors.
Familiarity with standard ceiling heights might have influenced beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
The study did not distinguish between visual and locomotive permeability in stimuli, which might have different impacts on beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions.
